The central question is whether sequentially stacking LoRA adapters (or similar PEFT modules) across tasks causes the frozen backbone's representation space to be progressively misaligned with what each new adapter expects — not because weights change, but because the effective input distribution to each adapter shifts as earlier adapters reshape activations. The key concepts are: adapter composition (how residual updates from multiple adapters accumulate in the forward pass), representation drift (the geometric displacement of token embeddings in intermediate layers across task boundaries), and collapse (when the effective rank of the representation manifold degrades, causing task-discriminative dimensions to merge or vanish). A beginner assumes that freezing the backbone guarantees stable representations; the expert knows that even frozen parameters produce different outputs when upstream adapters have altered the activation statistics that those parameters were calibrated against during pretraining — a form of implicit distribution shift with no gradient signal to correct it. Empirically, this layer-separation effect is substantial: Raghu et al.'s CKA analysis shows that representations at layers separated by 8+ transformer blocks in models like GPT-2-XL have CKA similarity below 0.3, suggesting that Fisher subspace overlap effectively vanishes at sufficient layer separation — implying that inserting adapter A at layer 8 and adapter B at layer 20 of a 32-layer model may require near-zero additional rank beyond what each task individually needs, a prediction consistent with MAD-X's empirical finding that language and task adapters can be stacked with minimal interference when positioned at alternating layer positions.
